catalog_quote: This work is based on the Copperbelt dialect.[fn.2] Like the majority of languages in this volume, Bemba is a tone language that does not have stress or any kind of accent marking. [...] [Sec. 2, prepub p.2] Bemba contrasts two level tones, high and low, which are generally phonologically treated as H vs. Ø following basic Bantu language assumptions (Kisseberth & Odden 2003). This means that phonologically low tones are not active and surface low-toned forms are considered to be lexically toneless but surface as low-toned if they are not affected by High tone spreading rules. [...] Vowels in Bemba can be short or long with the mora as the tone-bearing unit.[fn.4] [...] [Sec. 3, prepub p.10] Finally, although there is no penultimate lengthening in Bemba, there appears to be some lengthening of the final syllable in both the initial subject and the final constituent in the declarative sentence. We have not carried out systematic durational comparisons but notice it here and in figures discussed below. [...] [Philippson 1991, p.485] e) langues dans lesquelles la pénultième ne semble jouer aucun rôle, quel qu'il soit: ganda; bukusu; nyamwezi; bemba, tonga; kikuyu. [p.487] Au stade II, l'assimilation proximale a abouti à la neutralisation de l'opposition HH/HB, sans que soit encore atteint un vrai système accentuel; c'est le cas des langues de Tanzanie Occidentale: nyamwezi et sukuma, ainsi que du bemba.

sweep_summary: Bemba (bemb1257) is not in the catalog. works with stress in the title: (1)-(2) Hyman 1995 JALL 16:3-39 (two Glottolog records for the same paper) -- a prosodic-morphology (circumscription/minimality) analysis of perfective imbrication, not a stress source; no open copy exists (OpenAlex/S2 closed, De Gruyter bot-walled, absent from Hyman's Berkeley site); low priority. (3) Philippson 1991 Doctorat d'Etat thesis -- theses.fr marks it inaccessible and it is not on HAL, but the author's full PDF (542 pp., text) is on his DDL-Lyon page and is now. Bemba is one of its well-described sample languages and is explicitly classed as a tone language in which the penult plays no role and no true accentual system has emerged (pp. 91-92, 465, 485, 487). This corroborates the already-held deciding statement Kula & Hamann 2017 p. 1 ('Bemba is a tone language that does not have stress or any kind of accent marking'; no penultimate lengthening, p. 10), which I re-read from disk. Hyman 2013 (penultimate lengthening in Bantu) was checked and does not mention Bemba. no word stress (tone language).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bemba is described as a two-tone (H vs. toneless/L) language with contrastive vowel length and no word stress or accent of any kind; unlike many Eastern/Southern Bantu languages it also lacks phrase-penultimate lengthening (only an unquantified utterance-final-syllable lengthening is noted).

new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the language's prosodic system in general (word and phrase): no lexical stress, no accent, no penultimate-lengthening prominence at phrase level. Based on Copperbelt Bemba (Ndola) speakers; authors note tonal (not stress) differences between Copperbelt and Northern Bemba.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (and the JIPA Illustration) describe Copperbelt Bemba (Ndola speakers), an urban variety of bemb1257; Glottolog's Bemba (Zambia) bemb1257 covers both Northern ('standard', Kasama) and Copperbelt Bemba, which the authors say differ in tone-spreading rules but not (per their statement) in having stress. Distinct from Bembe/Beembe (bemb1255, beem1239) and from Town Bemba as a contact variety.

new_statements.reading: Bemba has no word stress and no accent of any kind; it is a pure two-tone (H/L, mora-TBU) language, without penultimate lengthening. Independently corroborated by the newly obtained Philippson 1991 thesis (author's PDF from DDL Lyon), which lists Bemba among the East African Bantu languages 'dans lesquelles la pénultième ne semble jouer aucun rôle, quel qu'il soit' (p. 485) and classes it as tonal, not having reached 'un vrai système accentuel' (p. 487; also p. 465 and pp. 91-92). If a catalog record is created, code Bemba as a tone language with no word stress (Copperbelt variety; Philippson's data are largely from Sharman/Meeussen and informants, i.e. Northern/standard Bemba as well).

tone_statements.quote: Ø indicates that the entire stem lacks an underlying high tone specification. Tone symbols used here—such as H, ꜜH, and L—stand for high, downstepped high, and low tones at the surface level, respectively. … nominal stems in CB are classified into two categories, i.e., one with no lexical high tone assigned, thus called Ø-toned nouns (or toneless nouns), and one with any lexical high tone assigned, labelled as Type-II … some of the HHL type nouns can be pronounced with a clear downstepped H on the final syllable, i.e., [HHꜜH].

tone_statements.quote: There are two level tones, which we will refer to as high and low, respectively. The contrastive nature of these tones follows from the observation of tonal minimal pairs, such as [luká] ‘weave!’ vs. [lúká] ‘vomit!’ (Bickmore and Kula 2013:104). We follow B&K in assuming that only high tones are active in the phonology … Because falling tones appear only on bimoraic syllables, we take the mora to be the TBU in CB, and we analyze a falling-toned syllable as one where only the first of two moras is associated with a high tone.

tone_statements.summary: Copperbelt Bemba: two level tones, high vs low (only H phonologically active); mora is the TBU, falling tone = H on first mora of a long vowel; ternary bounded H spread; downstep between H spans.

tone_statements.quote: We start with a discussion of some general tone facts of CB, and basic theoretical assumptions. In all respects, we closely follow B&K. There are two level tones, which we will refer to as high and low, respectively. We assume that only high level tones are active in the phonology, represented as tonal autosegments. [...] On long vowels, CB can display falling tones in addition to level tones. Rising tones are absent from the data. Because falling tone appears only on bimoraic syllables, we take the mora to be the TBU in CB, and we analyse a falling-toned syllable as one where only the first of two moras is associated with a high tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 64, section 3.2 'Ternarity in Copperbelt Bemba bounded tone spreading'
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones with only H active (privative H vs toneless), moraic TBU, falling but no rising contours on long vowels; lexical H sponsors undergo bounded ternary spreading sensitive to syllable weight, plus unbounded spreading in phrasal contexts.

tone_statements.citation: Breteler, Jeroen & René Kager. 2017. Layered feet laid bare in Copperbelt Bemba tone. Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 4 (AMP 2016). Washington, DC: Linguistic Society of America. doi:10.3765/amp.v4i0.4003.
tone_statements.quote: CB level tones come in two heights. Following Bickmore & Kula we take H to be the only active element in the phonology, with low level tones being the phonetic implementation of an absence of H. In addition to the level tones, long vowels permit falls, but not rises. Again following Bickmore & Kula, we analyse this by stating that the TBU in CB is the mora, meaning that a falling tone is the realization of a long vowel where only the first mora is associated to a high tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 2, sec. 2 'Ternarity in Copperbelt Bemba bounded tone spreading' (downstep: p. 3, sec. 2.2, ex. 9)
tone_statements.summary: Copperbelt Bemba: two tone heights, High vs low (low = absence of H); the mora is the TBU, falls on long vowels = H on the first mora only; bounded ternary H spreading; downstep between adjacent H spans.

tone_statements.citation: Kula, Nancy C. 2017. The conjoint/disjoint alternation and phonological phrasing in Bemba. In Jenneke van der Wal & Larry M. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. doi:10.1515/9783110490831-010 (Crossref dates the chapter 2016).
tone_statements.quote: The verbal tonology of Bemba distinguishes between lexically H-toned and toneless verb roots typically resulting in minimal pairs such as -lùk- ‘weave’ vs. -lúk- ‘vomit’. … The tone-bearing unit (TBU) in Bemba is the mora with the following tonal structures attested: Cà, Càà, Cá, Cáá, Cáà, *Càá. … In all examples high tone is marked by an acute accent and low tone with a grave accent. … a tautosyllabic LHH contour is created on the initial syllable. This resolves to a level H, as rising tones are prohibited in Bemba.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2 'Background: Basic Bemba tonology', author-MS (third sentence = fn. 3) + sec. 3 discussion of ex. (7d) (last sentence); printed volume pp. not shown in this copy
tone_statements.summary: Lexical H vs toneless (low) on the mora; HL falls on long vowels but no rising tones; bounded/unbounded H spreading, downstepped H after OCP violations, melodic and floating Hs; nothing on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Kula, Nancy C. & Bettina Braun. 2015. Mental representation of tonal spreading in Bemba: Evidence from elicited production and perception. Southern African Linguistics and Applied Language Studies 33(3): 307-323. doi:10.2989/16073614.2015.1108768.
tone_statements.quote: In this paper we investigate the mental representation of derived tones in Bemba, a Bantu language that has a two-way tone contrast but which shows robust tone spreading patterns. … Bantu languages generally have two tones (High and Low) and are renowned for having intricate tone spreading rules. … Lexical tone (High or Low) can be associated with the verb stem or with affixes preceding the verb stem. … Unbounded spreading spreads a H rightwards up to the end of the verb form, targeting all following toneless moras in a phrase-final word.
tone_statements.locator: Abstract, p. 1 + section 'Background on Bemba tone', p. 3
tone_statements.summary: Two-way tone contrast, High vs Low (lexically H vs toneless); H spreads rightward over toneless moras, unbounded or bounded (ternary in Copperbelt, binary in Northern Bemba); experimental study.

tone_statements.quote: Nouns functioning as head nouns of relative clauses can be distinguished by their tone marking. A word-final high (H) tone is found with restrictive relatives (12), while a final low (L) tone is found with non-restrictives (13). In both cases, the predicate of the relative clause is marked as being in a relative clause, as will be discussed in the following section.

tone_statements.summary: Two-way H vs L(unmarked) lexical/grammatical tone; word-final H~L on nouns and H~L on subject markers carry grammatical (relative-clause, restrictiveness) information.

tone_statements.citation: Kasonde, Alexander [Raymond Makasa] & M. Dunham. 2009. A Pedagogical Study of Tone Neutralization in Cibemba Phonetics and Phonology. African Research Review 3(1): 425-435. doi:10.4314/afrrev.v3i1.43589.
tone_statements.quote: The results show that distinctive low and high tone contrasts exist in Cibemba. (1) Cibemba H: amabala > a ma ba la ‘spots’ H.L.H.H L: amabala > a ma ba la ‘gardens’ L.H.L.L H: imba > i mba ‘(sg) sing!’ H.H L: imba > i mba ‘(sg) dig!’ L.H … By suggesting that a tone is either H or L, the study does not imply that the relative contrasts are absolute. The degree of pitch contrast always depends on the context. The context includes the type of consonant and vowel found in the syllable, expressiveness as well as syllable position and grammatical function.
tone_statements.locator: p. 430 (Results section, which begins p. 429; examples (1)-(2))
tone_statements.summary: Two contrastive tones, high and low, shown by minimal pairs (amabala 'spots' H.L.H.H vs 'gardens' L.H.L.L); the authors argue tone is largely phonetic and neutralised in context, e.g. in song.

tone_statements.citation: Yukawa, Yasutoshi (湯川恭敏). 1988. ベンバ語動詞アクセント試論 [A Tentative Tonal Analysis of Bemba Verbs] (含 付表動詞リスト). アジア・アフリカ言語文化研究 (Journal of Asian and African Studies) 36: 107-159. Tokyo: ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies.
tone_statements.quote: 正書法ではアクセント表記をしないことになっているが, この試論では, 高く発音される母音 (長母音の後半分も含む) および子音前鼻音の上に ´ をつけ, 低く発音されるそれらと区別する。長母音あるいは母音連続の後半部分の高低は有意味的である。子音前鼻音の高低は一般的には有意味的ではない (一般的には高い母音の直後で高い) が, §2-2-5 に見るように高低が有意味的であることもあるので, 高く発音されるものには ´ をつけることにする。 … ベンバ語の動詞は, アクセントの面から二つに分類される。その差異は不定形においても明確にあらわれる。
tone_statements.translation: The orthography does not mark accent, but in this essay an acute ´ is placed over vowels pronounced high (including the second half of long vowels) and over preconsonantal nasals, distinguishing them from those pronounced low. The high/low of the second half of a long vowel or vowel sequence is distinctive. The high/low of a preconsonantal nasal is generally not distinctive (generally it is high right after a high vowel), but as seen in §2-2-5 it can be distinctive, so those pronounced high are also marked with ´. … Bemba verbs are classified into two [types] with respect to accent. The difference appears clearly in the infinitive as well.
tone_statements.locator: p.108 right column ('はじめに', tone-marking conventions), and p.110 right column (§1-1 不定形)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Verb tone ('accent') analysed as high vs low pitch on each vowel, second half of long vowels counted separately; verbs fall into two lexical tone classes (A, B) with tense-by-tense patterns.

tone_statements.quote: Bemba, like Lamba, must be classed as a ‘“‘ Tone Language ’’ … In normal grammatical speech, Christopher used three level tones, a high tone (indicated by the diacritic! above the vowel), a mid-tone (unindicated), and a low tone (indicated by the diacritic ! beneath the vowel). In addition to these tones, we observed a falling tone used when two mid-tones were followed by a low tone. This we have considered unnecessary to mark … we do not consider its existence as sufficiently significant to necessitate special recording.

tone_statements.summary: Three level tones (high, mid, low) distinguish otherwise identical words; a falling tone in mid-mid-low sequences is not treated as distinctive; regular penultimate main stress described separately.

tone_statements.quote: In Copperbelt Bemba (Bickmore & Kula 2013, Kula & Bickmore 2015), underlying H tones undergo one of two spreading processes, bounded ternary spreading or unbounded spreading. [...] Bounded spreading obeys the Obligatory Contour Principle; it will spread up to two additional TBUs, maintaining at least one L TBU before the second H.

sources.quote: CB level tones come in two heights. tone.translation: The orthography does not mark accent, but in this essay an acute ´ is placed over vowels pronounced high (including the second half of long vowels) and over preconsonantal nasals, distinguishing them from those pronounced low. The high/low of the second half of a long vowel or vowel sequence is distinctive. The high/low of a preconsonantal nasal is generally not distinctive (generally it is high right after a high vowel), but as seen in §2-2-5 it can be distinctive, so those pronounced high are also marked with ´. … Bemba verbs are classified into two [types] with respect to accent. The difference appears clearly in the infinitive as well.

tone.quote: Bemba does not use stress but uses tone — using length and musical note. It should be mentioned that in tone, it is not just one syllable in each word that may be made long or high, it may be any number or none at all. When English words are borrowed into Bemba, the stressed syllables are realised by high tone and lengthened vowel. … in cases where there are two stresses, only the main stress is realized in Bemba as high tone. … The English stress is changed to high tone while unstressed syllables recieve alow tone in the loanwords.
